title: Manage Your Meraki Networks from Micetro

cta.text: See Micetro with your Meraki estate

prompt:
Product: BlueCat. Demo: "Manage Your Meraki Networks from Micetro".
Story: Manage Meraki DHCP and IPAM from Micetro
Once Meraki is connected, its networks, VLANs, clients and fixed IPs show up in Micetro. Watch a reservation and an excluded range get created in Micetro and written to Meraki. About 5 minutes.
Audience: network and DNS engineers and IT leaders evaluating the product. Tone: concise, confident, practical, no hype.
34 screenshots, keep this order, one tooltip per image, calling out the highlighted UI element:
1. Your Meraki branches sit in the same pane as your other networks: one source of truth. Switch to the flat view so one search can reach any of them.
2. Every network is now in one list. Use the quick filter to jump to the Helsinki branch.
3. Each Meraki network is a DHCP server and each VLAN is a scope. Point at the Guest VLAN row to reach its actions.
4. The row's menu button has appeared. Open it to find what Meraki holds for this VLAN.
5. Open the network to see its clients and fixed IPs as Micetro shows them.
6. Clients are leases, fixed IPs are reservations. Filter to one client's address to see what Micetro knows about it.
7. One Meraki client, shown as a lease. Select it to see its history.
8. History builds up as clients are synced. Next, find a free address to reserve for a new device.
9. This address is free. Select it so we can act on it.
10. With a free address selected, reserve it for a device that needs a fixed IP.
11. Give the reservation a name so the device is easy to recognize later.
12. Now the device's MAC address, which ties the fixed IP to the device.
13. Name and MAC are set. Create the reservation.
14. Micetro asks for a change comment, so every change carries its reason. Save it to commit the reservation.
15. Reserve it here and it is written to Meraki, with no trip to the Meraki dashboard. Go back to the network list to make a second change.
16. Back at the network list. Switch to the flat view again to find the same network.
17. Filter to the same network so we can change its address pools.
18. Hover the network row to bring up its menu.
19. Open the row menu; the address pools are managed from there.
20. Open the DHCP pools to keep a range out of what Meraki hands out.
21. These are the network's pools. Add an exclusion to hold a range for static devices.
22. Start with the first address of the range.
23. Then the last address of the range.
24. Confirm the range.
25. The range is listed as an exclusion. Save the pools to apply it.
26. Another change comment, so the exclusion has a recorded reason. Save it to commit.
27. Reserved ranges in Meraki appear as exclusions. Next, check the network's other settings.
28. Hover the row again to reach the scope options.
29. Open the scope options to see how Meraki's LAN properties surface here.
30. Meraki LAN properties like lease time are DHCP options here. Nothing to change, so close it.
31. Last stop: the audit trail. Hover the row once more to reach it.
32. Open the menu to find this network's history.
33. Open the history to see who changed what.
34. Every action is logged with an audit trail, so changes made here are accountable.
Close: Meraki DHCP, viewed and managed in the same pane as the rest of your network, with an audit trail.
End with a call to action: See Micetro with your Meraki estate.
